title: Tolerances and exceptions in agile
blurb: Explain where tolerances sit in a PRINCE2 Agile project, recognize a real exception, and know what happens once one is forecast.
question: A release burn-up forecasts that two Must-have features cannot be delivered by the end of the stage. Is this an exception, and what should happen?

teach.h: Manage by exception, the agile way
teach.body: Manage by exception still applies in PRINCE2 Agile, and the book sees it at the heart of letting people self-manage while governance stays in control. The twist is where the tolerance sits: agile allows tolerance on what is delivered and restricts tolerance on time and cost. Teams are free to flex scope inside agreed limits; only a forecast breach of those limits goes up a level.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 5.2.1.5, Table 5.1, Table 3.1

teach.body: An exception occurs when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded. It does not wait for the breach to happen. In agile it may be triggered by an updated burn chart at iteration or release level that shows progress heading outside tolerance. The guidance is to hold an immediate project meeting to discuss options before escalating to the project board. Typical triggers: the Must haves cannot all be delivered, or the MVP is forecast to arrive later than expected.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 12.1, Table 6.1, 9.4.2

children.label: Exception
children.sub: meet, then exception report to board

teach.caption: Musts not deliverable in the time and cost allowed = outside the flex = exception.

teach.body: Dropping a Could-have story to keep an iteration on time is the agreed flex, not an exception. A blocker the team can clear by swarming is handled at team level; if the team cannot resolve it, it goes to the project manager as an issue. Changes that do not affect the agreed baseline are handled informally at team level. Differences in agile maturity across team members are handled transparently, for example in retrospectives, not escalated.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 11.3.2, 11.4.2, Table 12.1, Table 5.1

teach.h: Inside the flex or an exception?
From burn chart to board decision

steps.label: Escalate
steps.sub: PM checks release map and canvas

teach.caption: Escalate issues and risks (controlling a stage, Table 13.9); authorize a stage or exception plan (directing a project, Table 13.4).

teach.body: In controlling a stage, the project manager examines the release map to see how far the deviation goes, works out recovery options, assesses them against the project canvas and the release map, and puts the situation, options and recommendation to the board in an exception report. The board, directing the project, can then review the updated project dashboard and approve an updated release map, or tell the project manager to close the project early.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.9, Table 13.4

levels.label: Product owner and team: work within

teach.body: Harrowfield's mortgage app project has a stage tolerance of zero on time and cost, with Musts fixed. Midway through the stage, project manager Ifeoma Adeyemi sees the release burn-up flatten: old payment code needs reworking, and the remaining Musts will not fit. She calls an immediate meeting with product owner Sean Doyle and the team to explore options, then sends the board an exception report recommending an updated release map. Earlier, when a Could had to move to a later release, nobody escalated.

teach.text: An EXCEPTION REPORT goes to the board when a stage or project plan is forecast to exceed tolerance. A highlight report (project dashboard) is regular status; an issue report covers one issue's impact and options. And the default answer to slippage is not 'add time': time and cost have zero tolerance.

items: Agile allows tolerance on what is delivered and restricts it on time and cost (Table 5.1).
An exception is a FORECAST breach of tolerance, not only an actual one.
Often triggered by an updated burn chart at iteration or release level.
Hold an immediate meeting on options before escalating to the board (Table 12.1).
Dropping Coulds, swarming on a blocker and detail changes are not exceptions.
PM escalates in an exception report; the board may approve an updated release map or premature closure.

summary: You can now explain why PRINCE2 Agile puts tolerance on what is delivered rather than on time and cost, and tell an exception from normal agile flex. You can also trace the path from an updated burn chart to an exception report and the board's decision.

A.q: When does an exception occur in a PRINCE2 Agile project?
options: When tolerances are forecast to be exceeded
When a Could-have story is dropped from an iteration
When a team's velocity falls in one iteration
When the product owner refines the product backlog
A.why: Table 12.1: an exception is likely when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded.

whyNot.1: Dropping a Could is the agreed flex in scope, not a breach of tolerance.
whyNot.2: A single dip in velocity may need attention but is not itself a forecast tolerance breach.
whyNot.3: Backlog refinement is routine product owner work, not an exception.

A.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, on which aspect does tolerance mainly sit, and on which is it restricted?
options: On time; restricted on scope
On what is delivered; restricted on time and cost
On cost; restricted on benefits and quality
On risk; restricted on what is delivered
A.why: Table 5.1 (manage by exception): agile allows tolerance on what is delivered and restricts tolerance on time and cost.

whyNot.0: This reverses the rule: time is restricted and scope is where the flex sits.
whyNot.2: Cost has zero tolerance on all levels of plan.
whyNot.3: What is delivered is where tolerance sits, not where it is restricted.

A.q: An updated release burn chart shows progress heading outside tolerance. What does PRINCE2 Agile suggest happens first?
options: Extend the release by one iteration
Record the slippage in the lessons log
Wait for the stage end to report it
Hold an immediate meeting to discuss options
A.why: Table 12.1: this could lead to an immediate project meeting to discuss options before escalating to the project board.

whyNot.0: Time has zero tolerance; extending the release is not the response.
whyNot.1: A lesson may be recorded later, but the forecast breach needs action now.
whyNot.2: Waiting delays the response; exceptions are raised when forecast.

B.q: A delivery team hits a technical blocker mid-iteration and the whole team swarms on it. What is this?
options: An exception to report to the board
A baseline change for the CPO to decide
An issue handled at team level
A risk to assess with the Agilometer
B.why: A blocker the team can clear by swarming is handled at team level; if it cannot be handled there, it goes to the PM as an issue (11.4.2, Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: No tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, so there is no exception.
whyNot.1: A blocker does not change the project backlog, so it is not a baseline change.
whyNot.3: The Agilometer assesses the risks of working in an agile way, not day-to-day blockers.

B.q: Significant technical debt means the remaining Must haves cannot be delivered within the stage. Which product should the project manager produce?
options: Highlight report
Exception report
Issue report
Lessons report
B.why: This is an exception (Musts cannot be delivered), so the PM informs the board in an exception report with options and a recommendation (9.4.2, Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: A highlight report (project dashboard) gives regular stage status, not a forecast breach.
whyNot.2: An issue report covers one issue's impact; a forecast breach of stage tolerance needs an exception report.
whyNot.3: A lessons report shares lessons; it does not escalate a breach.

B.q:
Which two statements about tolerances and exceptions in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. Manage by exception is at the heart of empowering people to self-manage.
2. The PM may extend the stage end date to protect the Must haves.
3. The MVP should be identified so an exception can be raised if it is forecast to be late.
4. Varying agile maturity across the team is escalated to the board.
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
B.why: Manage by exception is at the heart of empowering self-management (1), and the MVP is identified so an exception can be raised if it is forecast to be delivered late (3) (Table 5.1, Table 6.1).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: time has zero tolerance, so the PM cannot extend the stage.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: time is fixed, and varying maturity is handled transparently, not escalated.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: varying agile maturity is handled openly with the team, not escalated.

C.q: In controlling a stage, what does the project manager do when escalating a forecast breach of stage tolerance?
options: Updates the team dashboard and asks the PO to replan the iteration
Approves an exception plan and updates the project canvas
Raises a change request and waits for the CPO's decision
Assesses options against the project canvas and reports to the board
C.why: Escalate issues and risks: the PM examines the release map, assesses recovery options against the project canvas and release map, and recommends to the board in an exception report (Table 13.9).

whyNot.0: Team dashboards are updated by teams; a stage-level breach goes to the board.
whyNot.1: The board, not the PM, authorizes an exception plan in directing a project.
whyNot.2: A forecast stage breach is escalated to the board, not left with the CPO as a change request.

C.q: The board receives an exception report. In 'authorize a stage or exception plan', what can the board do?
options: Approve the updated release map or order premature closure
Extend the time tolerance and approve the next stage
Rewrite the team plans and reset team velocities
Replace the product owners and restart the stage
C.why: The board reviews the updated project dashboard and approves the updated release map, or instructs the PM to initiate premature closure (Table 13.4).

whyNot.1: Time has zero tolerance in PRINCE2 Agile; the board's options are the updated release map or closure.
whyNot.2: Team plans belong to the delivery teams, not the board.
whyNot.3: Replacing product owners is not the board's response to an exception report.

C.q: A team must drop one Could-have story to finish its iteration on time. Is this an exception, and why?
options: Yes, because the scope of the iteration has changed
Yes, because the work package description is now inaccurate
No, because flexing Coulds is inside the agreed tolerance
No, because iteration tolerances are set to zero scope
C.why: Scope is flexed for Should and Could haves, so dropping a Could is within tolerance; only a forecast breach is an exception (Table 3.1, Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: Scope changing within the flex is expected; it does not breach tolerance.
whyNot.1: The set of user stories already allows for Coulds to flex.
whyNot.3: Scope is the aspect that flexes; it is time and cost that have zero tolerance.

reteach.title: A satnav with a fixed arrival time
reteach.question: If you must arrive at 9 with a fixed fuel budget, when do you phone ahead?

blocks.h: Phone ahead when you forecast you will be late
blocks.body: You must arrive at 9 and you cannot buy more fuel. You may skip the coffee stop (a Could) without telling anyone. But the moment the satnav forecasts you will miss 9 even without stops, you pull over, think through options and phone ahead. That call is the exception report: made on a forecast, with options, before the breach actually happens.

blocks.text: An exception is raised on the forecast, not after the deadline has already gone.

explain.body: Agile allows tolerance on what is delivered and restricts it on time and cost (Table 5.1). Musts are fixed; Shoulds and Coulds flex (Table 3.1).

test.q: Which aspect is restricted rather than flexed under PRINCE2 Agile's view of manage by exception?
options: Should-have scope
Could-have scope
Time
Benefits above minimum viability
test.why: Agile restricts tolerance on time and cost and allows tolerance on what is delivered (Table 5.1).

whyNot.0: Should haves are part of the flexed scope.
whyNot.1: Could haves are the first scope to flex.

explain.body: An exception occurs when tolerances are FORECAST to be exceeded, often shown by an updated burn chart at iteration or release level (Table 12.1).

test.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. An exception occurs when tolerances are [?] to be exceeded.
options: agreed
forecast
allowed
requested
test.why: Table 12.1: an exception is likely when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded.

whyNot.0: Nobody agrees for tolerances to be exceeded; an exception is a forecast breach.
whyNot.2: Tolerances are not allowed to be exceeded; that is why the board is told.
whyNot.3: An exception is not requested; it arises from a forecast.

explain.h: Not every problem is an exception
explain.body: Swarming on a blocker, trading stories and dropping Coulds are team-level responses. Only a forecast breach of stage or project tolerance goes to the board.

test.q: Which situation is MOST likely to be an exception?
options: A Could-have story moves to the next release
The MVP is forecast to be delivered later than expected
The team swarms to clear a test environment blocker
A user asks for a small change within the backlog
test.why: The MVP is identified so that an exception can be raised if it is forecast to be delivered later than expected (Table 6.1).

whyNot.0: Moving a Could is the agreed flex in scope.
whyNot.2: Swarming handles a blocker at team level.
whyNot.3: A change within the backlog that does not affect the baseline is handled informally at team level.

explain.body: In escalate issues and risks, the PM puts the situation, options and recommendation to the board in an exception report, after assessing options against the project canvas and release map (Table 13.9).

test.q: Who produces the exception report, and for whom?
options: The PM, for the project board
The product owner, for the PM
Project assurance, for the CPO
The team coach, for the agile coach
test.why: The project manager produces the exception report to inform the project board of a forecast breach (Table 12.1, Table 13.9).

whyNot.1: Product owners raise issues to the PM; the exception report goes from PM to board.
whyNot.2: Project assurance advises on exception reports but does not produce them.
whyNot.3: Team coaches support teams; they do not produce exception reports.
